name: AI Drafting of Regulatory Documents
title: AI Drafting of Regulatory Documents
answer: Teams use AI to draft parts of investigational new drug applications, investigator brochures and nonclinical summaries, documents with rigid formats. One study reported nonclinical summary drafting fell from about 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours per batch with no critical regulatory errors under its criteria.

reading.body:
One study reported AI cut nonclinical summary drafting from about 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours per batch, with no critical regulatory errors under its criteria.

The pattern is narrow and specific. The documents named here, investigational new drug applications, investigator brochures and nonclinical summaries, have rigid formats and are assembled from source reports that already exist. That is the condition under which drafting compresses: the input is fixed, the output structure is fixed, and the work is condensation rather than invention. The reported reduction, from roughly 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours per batch, is large enough that it is better read as a change in what the task is than as an efficiency gain within the same task.

For AI scaling, the relevant point is where the time goes instead. The data states that savings rarely include review time, and that a pilot should be measured by total time including review and by the number and severity of errors found. So the honest unit of comparison is not drafting hours but drafting plus review, and the data does not give that combined figure. It also does not say how many documents were in a batch, which model or tool was used, who reviewed the output, or whether the no-critical-errors result holds outside the criteria that study applied.

What this does not tell the reader is whether the approach generalises. One study, one document type, one set of error criteria. Nothing here speaks to compute, buildings or power, and nothing should be inferred about them from this data. The practical instruction the data does support is procedural: run the pilot on your own documents, count the errors review finds, and treat the headline time saving as a claim to verify rather than a result to adopt.

The compression from 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours is not a speedup of the same activity. It is a change in what the writer does. When the input is a fixed set of source reports and the output is a fixed summary format, the drafting step becomes assembly, and assembly is what a model can do. The judgment that remains is whether the assembled text matches the source, preserves qualifications, and presents findings accurately. That judgment is review, and the data says review time is rarely included in the savings figure.

The comparison the data supports is between drafting time and total time, and only one of those two numbers is given. A team that adopts the headline figure without measuring review has adopted a number that describes half a process. The pilot instruction in the data exists precisely because the combined figure is not published here: measure total time including review, and measure the number and severity of errors found. Those two measurements, not the drafting hours, are what tell a team whether the approach works on its documents.

The error criterion matters as much as the time. The study reported no critical regulatory errors under its criteria, which is a statement about that study's definition of critical, not a general guarantee. A different document type, a different reviewer, or a stricter definition of critical could produce a different result. The data does not say how many documents were in a batch, which tool was used, or who reviewed the output, so none of those variables can be held constant when comparing this result to another.

What is an investigator brochure?

A document summarising clinical and nonclinical data on an investigational product for trial investigators. It is one of the document types named as suitable for AI drafting, alongside investigational new drug applications and nonclinical summaries.

How should a pilot be measured?

By total time including review, and by the number and severity of errors found. Drafting hours alone are not the measure, because the data states that reported savings rarely include review time.

Does the 100 hours to 3 to 4 hours figure include review time?

No. The data presents it as a drafting reduction and separately states that savings rarely include review time. The combined drafting plus review figure is not given.

How many documents are in a batch?

The data does not say. It reports the reduction per batch without defining batch size, so the figure cannot be converted into a per-document rate.

Which model or tool produced the result?

The data does not name one. It cites a single arXiv study, 2509.09738, dated September 2025, and gives no tool, vendor, or model.

Does the no-critical-errors finding apply to other document types?

The data does not establish that. The result is reported under that study's own criteria, and nothing here tests it against a different document type, reviewer, or definition of critical error.

AI for Evidence Dossiers and Literature Reviews

explainer:
Investigational new drug applications, investigator brochures and similar documents follow rigid structures and draw heavily on existing study reports. Writers spend much of their time condensing nonclinical and clinical findings into required summary formats.

AI drafting tools can produce first drafts of these summaries from source reports, and studies report large reductions in drafting time. The review burden remains: every summary must match the source, preserve qualifications and present findings accurately. Teams that pilot AI on their own document types, measuring both time saved and errors found in review, get a realistic picture before scaling.

What regulatory documents involve

A marketing application contains hundreds of documents: clinical overviews, summaries of safety and efficacy, module 2 summaries, responses to agency questions, labelling and periodic reports after approval. Much of the text is structured, follows templates, and restates data that already exists in study reports and databases. That is why drafting is one of the first regulatory tasks where language models have been tried.

Where models help and where they do not

Models are good at the first draft of templated sections, at turning a results table into prose, at checking that a document follows a required structure, and at drafting responses to routine agency questions from an existing evidence base. They are poor at judgement: deciding what the totality of evidence shows, choosing what to emphasise, and anticipating what a reviewer will challenge. Those remain the regulatory writer's job, and they are the parts that decide approvals.

Controls that regulators expect

Agencies have said that sponsors are responsible for submissions regardless of how they were drafted, and some ask for a description of AI use. The working practice is to keep source data traceable from every sentence, verify every number against its source table, have the scientific authors review machine drafted sections with the sections marked, and keep records showing the review happened. Companies also keep the models away from unpublished competitor data and from patient level data unless the environment is approved for it.
